newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea to open mutual fund business.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea to open mutual fund business.

text.p: South Korea said on Tuesday it would allow foreign investment houses to sell overseas mutual funds to domestic investors and buy into local mutual funds from December.

Indirectly, the move will give foreign investors greater access to the domestic stock market, but analysts said they did not anticipate big inflows or outflows of equity investment as a result of the liberalisation.

"I don't see any big fund flows resulting from the measure because of the weak interest among local investors in overseas equity investment and the sagging stock market here," said Lee Won-il, head of research at UBS Securities.

Foreign investment companies will be allowed to sell overseas mutual funds set up under laws of Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) member nations through public subscription.
South Korea was invited to join the Paris-based club of rich nations this month.
They will also be allowed to market offshore beneficiary certificates.
At the same time, foreign investors will be allowed to buy beneficiary certificates on up to 20 percent of the value of mutual funds issued by domestic investment firms.
Government officials and analysts said they expected the moves would help shake-up the domestic financial industry by adding competition.
"It will become a big step forward for the nation's financial industry," said Kim Kyung-hoh, director of the finance ministry's securities industry division.

"If the local bourse was on a bull run such a step could have led to a rush of foreign funds. But now we are not in such a situation," said Lee Won-hee, an executive director at Korea Investment Trust Co.

Foreign investors are now allowed to buy up to 20 percent of South Korean shares on the Seoul stock market, but foreign investment has been lacklustre mainly due to the languishing stock market, analysts said.
The Seoul stock market closed Tuesday's session at 766.32 points, down 22.4 percent from this year's highest close of 986.94 in early May.
Gloomy prospects for exports as a result of falling prices for major South Korean export items, including semiconductors, have depressed the stock market.

Also limiting the impact of the finance ministry move is the condition that sales in South Korea must be made through existing domestic investment companies and brokerages and branches of foreign brokerages, analysts said.
"I think that condition would be a big obstacle for foreign individual investors to get their hands on domestic certificates," said Lee of UBS.
"Marketing through other companies will mean higher commissions," he added.
